title: The More We Personalize Education, the More We Need Common Tests
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Aldeman takes New York's competency-based vision statement and shows that it becomes defensible with three words deleted. His distinction is between personalizing the route and personalizing the destination: students legitimately need different amounts of time, explanation and support, but that is not a reason to measure them against different standards. He accepts that instructional flexibility is now genuinely available, since online courses, ed-tech programs, AI tools and expanded school choice have made instruction less scarce than it once was, and argues the scarce good is now guidance and accountability rather than teaching itself. The counterintuitive move is the conclusion: the more a system personalizes, the more it needs a common assessment, because otherwise no one can tell whether flexible pacing produced different paths to the same standard or simply lowered the bar for some students. He then applies the same logic to a defense of test-blind admissions at the University of California, noting that record graduation rates say nothing about what graduates know. A short closing section points out that the college-level math gaps now being lamented were visible in eighth-grade data years earlier.
points: Separates flexibility in pacing and support from flexibility in outcomes, and argues only the first is a legitimate form of personalization.
Recommends concrete state moves that do not require overnight redesign: easier course testing out, relaxed seat-time rules, and permission to experiment with pacing and grouping.
Inverts the usual assumption by arguing that personalization raises rather than lowers the value of common assessments.
Treats record graduation rates as evidence of a measurement failure rather than a success when students arrive unable to do basic math.
Notes that the college math problem was already visible in the same students' eighth-grade results, making it predictable and preventable.
quotes: Did you catch that? Rather than personalizing pacing and outcomes, the state should keep a common benchmark while allowing for flexibility. It’s a simple but important change, and I think it reflects one thing the field is getting wrong about personalization.

Students are different. Children enter school with different skills, have different interests, and need different amounts of explanation and practice. That’s an argument for giving students different amounts of time and support to meet the same expectations, not for measuring their learning against different standards.
That kind of personalization is becoming increasingly possible. Instruction is no longer as scarce as it once was.
It would be folly for a state to try to impose a personalization model on every school tomorrow. Most schools aren’t set up to reorganize this dramatically overnight.
But state leaders could make it easier for students to test out of courses and advance when they’re ready, relax seat-time requirements, and let schools experiment with flexible pacing and grouping.

And the more schools personalize instruction like this, the more important common assessments become. Otherwise, states won’t be able to tell whether personalization produced different routes to the same standard, or if some students are just being held to different standards.

Graduation rates tell us how many students received degrees, but they don’t tell us what those students know. With some students arriving on campus unable to do basic math, pointing to record-high graduation rates doesn’t answer that concern.
This problem is predictable and preventable, and yet someone has to step in and actually prevent it.
